Simulated RD-DID panel (running variable moves over time)

Source: R/data.R
rddid_sim_pv.Rd

The same design as rddid_sim (confounding jump 0.5 in every year, treatment effect 1 in year 3), except that each unit's running variable drifts between years (an independent normal deviation from the unit's base position, with standard deviation 0 in year 1, 0.15 in year 2 and 0.30 in year 3), so some units are above the cutoff in one year and below it in another. These "switchers" are what the tests of the assumptions (rd_typecont(), rd_compstable(), rd_homog(), rd_trendcell()) examine, and they make the sampling scheme "panel, running variable varies over time".

Usage

rddid_sim_pv

Format

A data frame with 3,000 rows and the same 6 columns as rddid_sim.

Source

Generated by data-raw/make_sim.R (seed 20261027, chosen with data-raw/seed_scan.R so that the assumptions that hold are comfortably not rejected and the one that fails clearly is).

Details

By design, composition stability fails here: because the spread of the deviations grows with the year, the mix of units near the cutoff (who was above the cutoff in another year) is not the same in every year, and rd_compstable() rejects. The confounding jump is nevertheless the same for every unit, so homogeneous confounding holds (rd_homog() does not reject) and rddid() still recovers the effect of 1. Type continuity and the constant within-type jump also hold.

See also

rddid_sim.

Examples

# units that change side of the cutoff between years
sw <- tapply(rddid_sim_pv$V, rddid_sim_pv$id, function(v) length(unique(v)) > 1)
sum(sw)
#> [1] 176
rd_typecont(rddid_sim_pv, x = "R", time = "year", id = "id")
#> Test of a continuous type distribution  [rd_typecont()]
#>   H0: the share of each type jumps by zero at the cutoff, in every period
#>   Sampling scheme: panel, running variable varies over time (detected from the data)
#>   Periods: 1, 2, 3   Types: ++, +-, -+, --   Bandwidth: CCT MSE-optimal, chosen per cell
#> 
#>   Joint Wald chi-squared(9) = 4.782,  p = 0.853
#>     Period 1: chi-squared(3) = 1.531,  p = 0.675
#>     Period 2: chi-squared(3) = 0.382,  p = 0.944
#>     Period 3: chi-squared(3) = 2.202,  p = 0.532
